claim: Amputees experiencing highly vivid phantom sensations maintain cortical representation of their missing hand.
source: Previously we showed that amputees experiencing highly vivid phantom sensations maintain cortical representation of their missing hand (Kikkert et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kikkert et al., 2016

claim: Key aspects of acquired amputees' missing hand representation persisted, despite varying vividness of phantom sensations.
source: We found that key aspects of acquired amputees' missing hand representation persisted, despite varying vividness of phantom sensations.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from RSA analysis in the study

claim: Missing hand representation of congenital one-handers was significantly reduced compared to acquired amputees.
source: In contrast, missing hand representation of congenital one-handers, who do not experience phantom sensations, was significantly reduced.
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing groups

claim: Individuals' reported motor control over their phantom hand positively correlated with the extent to which their somatosensory hand representation was normally organised.
source: Across acquired amputees, individuals' reported motor control over their phantom hand positively correlated with the extent to which their somatosensory hand representation was normally organised.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis between kinaesthesia and typicality

claim: Once cortical organisation is formed, it is remarkably persistent, despite long-term attenuation of peripheral signals.
source: We conclude that once cortical organisation is formed, it is remarkably persistent, despite long-term attenuation of peripheral signals.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental findings across groups

claim: Adjacent body parts are represented more proximally on the cortical sheet than those further apart in primary somatosensory cortex.
source: A fundamental organising principle in the primary somatosensory cortex (SI) is somatotopic mapping, where adjacent body parts are represented more proximally on the cortical sheet than those further apart (Penfield and Rasmussen, 1950).
evidence: Supported by citation to Penfield and Rasmussen, 1950

claim: Neighbouring digits on the hand are represented closer together on the neocortex than non-neighbouring digits.
source: In the cortical hand area, this topographic organising principle results in a detailed digit map (Kaas et al., 1979; Penfield and Rasmussen, 1950), where neighbouring digits on the hand are represented closer together on the neocortex than non-neighbouring digits, as can be shown with functional MRI (fMRI) (Kolasinski et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kaas et al., 1979; Penfield and Rasmussen, 1950; Kolasinski et al., 2016

claim: Cortical activity patterns for neighbouring fingers overlap more than non-neighbouring fingers, independent of the exact spatial arrangement.
source: More generally, cortical activity patterns for neighbouring fingers overlap more – and are therefore more similar – than non-neighbouring fingers, independent of the exact spatial arrangement of these patterns (Ejaz et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ejaz et al., 2015

claim: The representational structure reflects the natural statistics of hand use over one's life course.
source: The representational structure (i.e. the relative dissimilarity of activity patterns for different movements) is thought to reflect the natural statistics of hand use over one's life course (Graziano and Aflalo, 2007; Overduin et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citations to Graziano and Aflalo, 2007; Overduin et al., 2012

claim: Concurrent inputs to neighbouring digits will increase representational similarity.
source: Concurrent inputs to neighbouring digits will increase representational similarity (Wang et al., 1995)
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 1995

claim: Greater individuation of inputs will induce greater representational dissimilarity.
source: while greater individuation of inputs will induce greater representational dissimilarity (Ejaz et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ejaz et al., 2015

claim: Alterations of inter-digit representational boundaries after the hand map has been formed can disrupt perception and action in musician's dystonia.
source: Some have even suggested that alterations of these inter-digit representational boundaries after the hand map has been formed, for example due to digit overuse, can disrupt (musician's dystonia [Elbert et al., 1998], but see Ejaz et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to Elbert et al., 1998, with caveat from Ejaz et al., 2016

claim: Alterations of inter-digit representational boundaries can improve perception and action in tactile discrimination.
source: or improve perception and action (tactile discrimination [Recanzone et al., 1992; Pleger et al., 2003]).
evidence: Supported by citations to Recanzone et al., 1992; Pleger et al., 2003

claim: Structured input from the periphery is not required for preserving sensorimotor hand representation.
source: We (Kikkert et al., 2016) and others (Flesher et al., 2016; Bruurmijn et al., 2017) recently challenged the view that structured input from the periphery is required for preserving sensorimotor hand representation (Dempsey-Jones et al., 2016; see also Davis et al., 1998, Mercier et al., 2006, Garbarini et al., 2018 for related brain stimulation and behavioural findings).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies including Kikkert et al., 2016; Flesher et al., 2016; Bruurmijn et al., 2017

claim: Some amputees report being able to volitionally move their phantom hand, resulting in kinaesthetic phantom sensations.
source: We took advantage of a well-documented phenomenon whereby some amputees report being able to volitionally move their phantom hand, resulting in kinaesthetic phantom sensations (Henderson and Smyth, 1948).
evidence: Supported by citation to Henderson and Smyth, 1948

claim: Phantom limb movements elicit both central and peripheral motor signals that are different from those found during movement imagery.
source: Phantom limb movements have been shown to elicit both central and peripheral motor signals that are different from those found during movement imagery (Reilly et al., 2006; Raffin et al., 2012a; Raffin et al., 2012b; Makin et al., 2013b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Reilly et al., 2006; Raffin et al., 2012a; Raffin et al., 2012b; Makin et al., 2013b

claim: Three amputees experiencing exceptionally vivid phantom sensations maintained digit selectivity, digit order, and extent of missing hand maps in SI similar to controls.
source: Using 7T imaging we explored whether three amputees experiencing exceptionally vivid phantom sensations maintained the canonical hand representation, exemplified by somatotopically organised representation of individual digits. We found that although digit selectivity was reduced, digit order and the extent of the missing hand maps in SI were similar to what is observed in controls.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from previous 7T imaging study

claim: All participants, including congenital one-handers, were able to engage the missing/nondominant hand area to some degree.
source: Overall, all participants, including congenital one-handers, were able to engage the missing/nondominant hand area to some degree.
evidence: Supported by univariate activity analysis in the study

claim: Activity in SI for the congenital one-handers' missing hand was reduced compared to controls (t(23)=3.5, p=0.002).
source: Although activity was reduced in SI for the congenital one-handers' missing hand compared to controls (t(23)=3.5, p=0.002)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Activity in SI for the congenital one-handers' missing hand was significantly greater than baseline (t(12)=2.6, p=0.02).
source: activity was significantly greater than baseline (t(12)=2.6, p=0.02).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Mean dissimilarity in amputees was slightly, though inconclusively, reduced compared to controls (t(28)=1.13, p=0.27, BF = 0.772).
source: In amputees, mean dissimilarity was slightly, though inconclusively, reduced compared to controls (t(28)=1.13, p=0.27, BF = 0.772)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Mean dissimilarity in amputees was significantly greater than in congenital one-handers (t(29)=3.54, p=0.001).
source: but significantly greater than in congenital one-handers (t(29)=3.54, p=0.001).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Congenital one-handers showed no differentiation between digits of their missing hand.
source: Congenital one-handers showed no differentiation between digits of their missing hand (mean dissimilarity not different from 0; t(12)=.73, p=0.48)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Dissimilarity in congenital one-handers was significantly reduced compared to controls (t(23)=4.86, p<0.001).
source: and dissimilarity was significantly reduced compared to controls (t(23)=4.86, p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: In amputees, typicality was high (rho = 0.75) and was not significantly different from controls (t(28)=.991, p=0.33, BF = 0.128).
source: In amputees, on average, typicality was high (rho = 0.75) and was not significantly different from controls (t(28)=.991, p=0.33, BF = 0.128).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: The organisation of digit representation after hand-loss remained statistically unchanged, after an average of 18 years of handlessness.
source: Hence, the organisation of digit representation after hand-loss remained statistically unchanged, after an average of 18 years of handlessness.
evidence: Inference drawn from typicality analysis

claim: Congenital one-handers' missing hand representation did not correlate with a normal hand pattern, reflected in diminished representational typicality (mean rho = 0.29).
source: As expected, congenital one-handers' missing hand representation did not correlate with a normal hand pattern, reflected in diminished representational typicality (mean rho = 0.29)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Congenital one-handers showed significantly lower typicality compared to both controls (t(23)=5.86, p<0.001) and amputees (t(29)=6.09, p<0.001).
source: compared to both controls (t(23)=5.86, p<0.001) and amputees (t(29)=6.09, p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Digit individuation in M1 was weaker than in SI.
source: The results in M1 were generally in line with our findings in SI, but, as expected (Ejaz et al., 2015; Bruurmijn et al., 2017), digit individuation was weaker
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citations to Ejaz et al., 2015; Bruurmijn et al., 2017

claim: Univariate activity in congenital one-handers' M1 was not significantly reduced compared to controls (t(23)=2.00, p=0.058).
source: Univariate activity in congenital one-handers' M1 was not significantly reduced compared to controls (t(23)=2.00, p=0.058)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Univariate activity in congenital one-handers' M1 was greater than baseline (t(12)=4.60, p=0.001).
source: and greater than baseline (t(12)=4.60, p=0.001).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Congenital one-handers showed significantly lower dissimilarity in M1 compared to controls (t(23)=4.23, p<0.001).
source: Congenital one-handers showed significantly lower dissimilarity compared to controls (t(23)=4.23, p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: In M1, mean dissimilarity in amputees was slightly reduced compared to controls, but these differences were not significant (t(28)=.53, p=0.60, BF = 0.325).
source: In amputees, mean dissimilarity was slightly reduced compared to controls, but these differences were not significant (t(28)=.53, p=0.60, BF = 0.325).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Typicality in M1 was significantly lower in congenital one-handers than in either controls (t(23)=3.42, p=0.002) or amputees (t(29)=3.50, p=0.002).
source: Typicality was also significantly lower in congenital one-handers than in either controls (t(23)=3.42, p=0.002) or amputees (t(29)=3.50, p=0.002)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Typicality in M1 was not different between amputees and controls (t(28)=.11, p=0.91, BF = 0.253).
source: while the latter groups were not different from each other (t(28)=.11, p=0.91, BF = 0.253).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: The correlation between odd and even RDMs was significantly lower in congenital one-handers (rho = -.02) compared to both amputees (rho = 0.41; p1H-AMP=.001) and controls (rho = 0.52; p1H-CTR=.001).
source: The correlation between odd and even RDMs was significantly lower in congenital one-handers (rho = -.02) compared to both amputees (rho = 0.41; p1H-AMP=.001) and controls (rho = 0.52; p1H-CTR=.001).
evidence: Supported by split-half reliability analysis

claim: There is no strongly consistent digit information in the missing hand area of congenital one-handers during this task.
source: Nevertheless, the relative reduction in split-half consistency indicates that there is no strongly consistent digit information in the missing hand area of congenital one-handers during this task.
evidence: Inference drawn from split-half reliability analysis

claim: Kinaesthesia of phantom sensations was the only significant predictor of typicality in the final regression model (β = 0.07, t = 4.46, p<0.001).
source: The final model (F = 19.9, p<0.001, adjusted R2 = 0.645 included only kinaesthesia of phantom sensations (β = 0.07, t = 4.46, p<0.001) and the intercept (β = 0.52, t = 8.89, p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by stepwise regression analysis

claim: Bootstrapping analysis returned kinaesthesia as the final variable in 96.3% of the iterations.
source: This bootstrapping analysis returned kinaesthesia as the final variable in 96.3% of the iterations (final model fit: median adjusted R2 = 0.645; 95% CI: 30-99%).
evidence: Supported by bootstrapping analysis

claim: There was a significant correlation between typicality and kinaesthesia in amputees (rho = 0.72, df = 16, p=0.001).
source: Post-hoc analysis confirmed a significant correlation between typicality and kinaesthesia in amputees (Figure 2A; rho = 0.72, df = 16, p=0.001).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis and shown in Figure 2A

claim: No significant correlation was found between typicality and nonpainful phantom vividness (rho = 0.13, df = 16, p=0.61).
source: No significant correlation was found with nonpainful phantom vividness (the chronicity of experiencing the missing hand as existing; Figure 2B; rho = 0.13, df = 16, p=0.61)
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis and shown in Figure 2B

claim: No significant correlation was found between typicality and years since amputation (rho = 0.17, df = 16, p=0.49).
source: or years since amputation (rho = 0.17, df = 16, p=0.49).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis

claim: The correlation between kinaesthesia and dissimilarity in SI approached significance (rho = 0.447, p=0.063).
source: The correlation between kinaesthesia and dissimilarity in SI approached significance (rho = 0.447, p=0.063).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis

claim: The correlation between kinaesthesia and typicality remained significant in SI after accounting for typicality in M1 as a covariate (F = 17.73, p<0.001, Adjusted R2 = 0.51; βKinaesthesia =.74, p<0.001).
source: Further analysis confirmed that the correlation between kinaesthesia and typicality remained significant in SI after accounting for typicality in M1 (mean rho = 0.44) as a covariate (F = 17.73, p<0.001, Adjusted R2 = 0.51; βKinaesthesia =.74, p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by partial correlation analysis

claim: The strong correlation between kinaesthesia and typicality in SI does not merely reflect information in M1.
source: This analysis suggests that although better recruitment of M1 is expected in individuals with clearer kinaesthetic sensations, the strong correlation between kinaesthesia and typicality in SI does not merely reflect information in M1.
evidence: Inference drawn from partial correlation analysis

claim: The regression line between kinaesthesia and typicality had an intercept of βintercept=.52.
source: As stated above, the regression line between kinaesthesia and typicality had an intercept of βintercept=.52.
evidence: Supported by regression analysis

claim: Even amputees who do not experience any phantom sensations will retain some typical missing hand representation.
source: These results predict that even amputees who do not experience any phantom sensations will retain some typical missing hand representation.
evidence: Prediction based on regression intercept analysis

claim: Three amputees with weak to no chronic phantom vividness (below 10/100) showed high typicality (average typicality (rho) = 0.83).
source: To test this prediction directly, we examined the three amputees in our dataset showing weak to no chronic phantom vividness (below 10/100). Despite not being able to experience clearly their phantom hand when performing the phantom movements task, these individuals showed high typicality (average typicality (rho) = 0.83).
evidence: Supported by analysis of subset of amputees

claim: Amputees with diminished phantom sensations showed significantly stronger correlations with the canonical hand structure than congenital one-handers (Mann-Whitney U = 38, p=0.007).
source: Moreover, when comparing their typicality to that found in the congenital one-handers (who were arguably better matched to this sub-group in terms of task demands), the amputees with diminished phantom sensations showed significantly stronger correlations with the canonical hand structure (Mann-Whitney U = 38, p=0.007).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison

claim: Typicality was not different between three amputees with diminished phantom sensations and controls (Mann-Whitney U = 29, p=0.52, BF = 0.089).
source: Typicality was not different between these three amputees and controls (Mann-Whitney U = 29, p=0.52, BF = 0.089).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison

claim: The representational structures' typicality in SI of amputees is still present in those with little to no phantom or kinaesthetic sensations.
source: Together, these additional analyses confirm that the representational structures' typicality in SI of amputees is still present in those with little to no phantom or kinaesthetic sensations.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from subset analysis

claim: It is possible that congenital one-handers have typical sensorimotor representation of their missing hand, but they did not access it due to unnatural task demands.
source: Indeed, it is possible that congenital one-handers have typical sensorimotor representation of their missing hand, but they did not access it due to unnatural task demands (see Striem-Amit et al., 2015 for analogous results regarding visual cortex organisation in congenitally blind individuals).
evidence: Speculation with supporting citation to Striem-Amit et al., 2015

claim: Finger movements lead to individuated digit representation in specific cortical patches in ipsilateral M1 and SI in two-handed controls.
source: In two-handed controls, finger movements lead to individuated digit representation in specific cortical patches in ipsilateral M1 and SI, which tightly correspond to the activity patches engaged in the movement of the mirror-symmetric contralateral finger (Diedrichsen et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Diedrichsen et al., 2013

claim: Ipsilateral digit representation fully overlaps with the representation of the contralateral hand.
source: Importantly, this ipsilateral digit representation fully overlaps with the representation of the contralateral hand (Diedrichsen et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Diedrichsen et al., 2018

claim: Ipsilateral representation disappears completely during asymmetric bimanual finger movements.
source: Furthermore, ipsilateral representation disappears completely during asymmetric bimanual finger movements, during which activity in M1 and SI is fully determined by the contralateral hand (Diedrichsen et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Diedrichsen et al., 2013

claim: The ipsilateral representation of one hand is likely elicited due to recruitment of the representation of the contralateral hand.
source: As such, the ipsilateral representation of one hand is likely elicited due to recruitment of the representation of the contralateral hand (Diedrichsen et al., 2018; Berlot et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Diedrichsen et al., 2018; Berlot et al., 2018

claim: All three groups were able to perform the individuated digit movement task equally well.
source: Importantly, all three groups were able to perform the individuated digit movement task equally well and contralateral representation of the intact hand was typical in all groups (see Materials and methods).
evidence: Supported by behavioral analysis

claim: Contralateral representation of the intact hand was typical in all groups.
source: Importantly, all three groups were able to perform the individuated digit movement task equally well and contralateral representation of the intact hand was typical in all groups (see Materials and methods).
evidence: Supported by RSA analysis

claim: Persistent missing hand representation in amputees should result in similar ipsilateral representation in their missing hand cortex as controls.
source: We predicted that persistent missing hand representation in amputees should result in similar ipsilateral representation in their missing hand cortex as controls.
evidence: Prediction based on theoretical framework

claim: If missing hand representation is diminished in congenital one-handers, then ipsilateral representation of their intact hand should show reduced representational features compared to those found in amputees.
source: If missing hand representation is diminished in congenital one-handers, then ipsilateral representation of their intact hand (in the missing hand area) should show reduced representational features compared to those found in amputees
evidence: Prediction based on theoretical framework

claim: Mean ipsilateral digit dissimilarity was not significantly different between amputees and controls (t(28)=1.42, p=0.166, BF = 0.209).
source: Mean (intact hand) ipsilateral digit dissimilarity and typicality were not significantly different between amputees and controls (Figure 3; dissimilarity: t(28)=1.42, p=0.166, BF = 0.209
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 3

claim: Mean ipsilateral typicality was not significantly different between amputees and controls (t(28)=.69, p=0.498, BF = 0.244).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 3

claim: Ipsilateral representation in congenital one-handers was significantly lower than in amputees for both dissimilarity (t(29)=3.81, p<0.001) and typicality (t(29)=3.05, p=0.005).
source: In contrast, ipsilateral representation in congenital one-handers was significantly lower than in amputees (dissimilarity: t(29)=3.81, p<0.001; typicality: t(29)=3.05, p=0.005)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis

claim: Ipsilateral representation in congenital one-handers showed similar trends versus controls for dissimilarity (t(23)=2.20, p=0.038) and typicality (t(23)=2.19, p=0.039).
source: and showed similar trends versus controls (dissimilarity: t(23)=2.20, p=0.038; typicality: t(23)=2.19, p=0.039).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis

claim: The cross-validated dissimilarity measurement in congenital one-handers was significantly larger than zero (t(12)=2.51, p=0.027).
source: The cross-validated dissimilarity measurement in this group was significantly larger than zero (t(12)=2.51, p=0.027)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis

claim: Congenital one-handers showed no significant differences in representation between SI and V5 for dissimilarity (t(12)=-1.03, p=0.322) and typicality (t(12)=.78, p=0.448).
source: Congenital one-handers showed no significant differences in representation between SI and V5 (dissimilarity: t(12)=-1.03, p=0.322; typicality: t(12)=.78, p=0.448)
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison between ROIs

claim: Both amputees and controls showed significant differences in representation between SI and V5 (all p's < 0.02).
source: whereas both amputees and controls showed significant differences (all p's < 0.02)
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison between ROIs

claim: There was a significant group x area interaction for dissimilarity (F(2,85)=4.25, p=0.018) and typicality (F(2,85)=4.42, p=0.015).
source: resulting in a significant group x area interaction (dissimilarity: F(2,85)=4.25, p=0.018; typicality: F(2,85)=4.42, p=0.015; Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by ANOVA analysis and shown in Figure 3

claim: The digit dissimilarity values in congenital one-handers are likely not specifically indicative of sensorimotor representation, but may rather reflect other task demands.
source: These findings corroborate that the digit dissimilarity values in congenital one-handers are likely not specifically indicative of sensorimotor representation, but may rather reflect other task demands.
evidence: Inference drawn from comparison with V5

claim: Amputees show individuated digit representation for their missing hand, as exemplified by significantly greater inter-digit dissimilarity values in amputees versus congenital one-handers.
source: Here, we demonstrated long-term stability of SI hand representation in a group of acquired amputees with diverse phantom sensations, including those experiencing limited phantom sensations. Using RSA, we find that amputees show individuated digit representation for their missing hand, as exemplified by significantly greater inter-digit dissimilarity values in amputees versus congenital one-handers.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings

claim: The inter-digit pattern comprising the missing hand representation was typical to SI hand representation in amputees and was not significantly different from controls.
source: The inter-digit pattern comprising the missing hand representation was typical to SI hand representation in amputees and was not significantly different from controls (as supported by a Bayesian analysis).
evidence: Summary of experimental findings with Bayesian support

claim: Stable hand representation was confirmed even after phantom sensations have diminished.
source: Importantly, by studying individuals with a varying range of phantom sensations, we were able to confirm stable hand representation even after phantom sensations have diminished.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings

claim: The persistent hand representation observed in amputees does not reflect mere cognitive task demands.
source: This result confirms that the persistent hand representation observed in amputees does not reflect mere cognitive task demands (e.g. visual feedback, Kuehn et al., 2018; or attention, Puckett et al., 2017).
evidence: Inference from comparison with congenital one-handers, with supporting citations

claim: Early-life experience is potentially necessary to create typical functional sensory organisation, but not to maintain it.
source: Bearing this caveat in mind, our findings suggest that early-life experience is potentially necessary to create typical functional sensory organisation, but not to maintain it.
evidence: Inference drawn from comparison between acquired amputees and congenital one-handers

claim: Restored peripheral input via hand transplantation or targeted reinnervation can reinstate sensorimotor hand representation.
source: It has previously been shown that restored peripheral input, for example via hand transplantation (Frey et al., 2008) or targeted reinnervation (Serino et al., 2017) can reinstate sensorimotor hand representation
evidence: Supported by citations to Frey et al., 2008 and Serino et al., 2017

claim: The canonical hand representation is, to an extent, immutable to change.
source: indicating that the canonical hand representation is, to an extent, immutable to change.
evidence: Inference from studies on restored peripheral input

claim: The SI hand map can persist independently of the original peripheral input, as observed in a patient sustaining a brachial plexus avulsion injury.
source: Moreover, we reported that the SI hand map can persist independently of the original peripheral input, as observed in a patient sustaining a brachial plexus avulsion injury, abolishing communication between the periphery and the central nervous system (Kikkert et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kikkert et al., 2016

claim: Amputees showed, on average, persistent SI representation despite suffering diverse nerve injuries spanned varying degrees of amputation.
source: Similarly, in the current study amputees showed, on average, persistent SI representation despite suffering diverse nerve injuries spanned varying degrees of amputation (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and Table 1

claim: The SI representation pattern is likely driven by motor efferent inputs.
source: Considering that our task required active phantom movements, it is likely that the SI representation pattern is driven by motor efferent inputs.
evidence: Inference based on task design

claim: The motor cortex in amputees remains functional.
source: Indeed, while motor signals can no longer reach their final output muscle terminal, the motor cortex in amputees remains functional (Raffin et al., 2012a; see Kokotilo et al., 2009 for similar results in spinal cord injury patients).
evidence: Supported by citations to Raffin et al., 2012a and Kokotilo et al., 2009

claim: When a motor command is sent out, efference signals are thought to reach SI and generate corollary discharge, suggested to resemble the expected sensory feedback activity pattern.
source: When a motor command is sent out (e.g. in the form of an attempted hand movement), efference signals are thought to reach SI and generate corollary discharge, suggested to resemble the expected sensory feedback activity pattern, resulting from the movement (London and Miller, 2013; Adams et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to London and Miller, 2013; Adams et al., 2013

claim: Congenital one-handers have never operated a hand, so the sensorimotor predictive coding architecture likely never formed in the first place.
source: Since congenital one-handers have never operated a hand, it is likely that this sensorimotor predictive coding architecture never formed in the first place, explaining the lack of inter-digit dissimilarity found in the present study.
evidence: Inference based on experimental findings and theoretical framework

claim: Sensory deprivation causes cortical reorganisation.
source: Since the pioneering work of Hubel and Wiesel, demonstrating that input loss to visual cortex in early development leads to profound physiological changes (Wiesel and Hubel, 1965b; Hubel and Wiesel, 1965; Wiesel and Hubel, 1965a), it has long been established that sensory deprivation causes cortical reorganisation.
evidence: Supported by citations to Wiesel and Hubel, 1965b; Hubel and Wiesel, 1965; Wiesel and Hubel, 1965a

claim: Deprivation-driven reorganisation following peripheral input-loss also occurs in adults.
source: Later seminal electrophysiological studies in monkeys further demonstrated that deprivation-driven reorganisation following peripheral input-loss also occurs in adults (Kaas et al., 1983).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kaas et al., 1983

claim: Following peripheral deafferentation of the hand and arm, the missing hand SI area becomes responsive to touch applied to the monkey's lower face.
source: For example, following peripheral deafferentation of the hand and arm, the missing hand SI area becomes responsive to touch applied to the monkey's lower face (Pons et al., 1991), likely due to subcortical re-routing of inputs (Kambi et al., 2014; Liao et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pons et al., 1991; Kambi et al., 2014; Liao et al., 2016

claim: Recent research indicates extensive reorganisation of multiple body-part representations onto the deprived hand area of congenital one-handers.
source: Recent research in humans indicates extensive reorganisation of multiple body-part representations onto the deprived hand area of congenital one-handers (Hahamy et al., 2017; Striem-Amit et al., 2018; Stoeckel et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hahamy et al., 2017; Striem-Amit et al., 2018; Stoeckel et al., 2009

claim: Original reports emphasised facial remapping in SI as a driving mechanism for phantom limb pain in amputees.
source: In amputees sustaining input loss in adulthood, original reports emphasised facial remapping in SI, akin to the reorganisation observed in monkeys (Flor et al., 1995), as a driving mechanism for phantom limb pain (maladaptive plasticity; Flor et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Flor et al., 1995 and Flor et al., 2006

claim: Later research challenged the notion that the deprived hand area gets taken over by facial inputs.
source: Later research challenged the notion that the deprived hand area gets taken over by facial inputs (Makin et al., 2013b; Makin et al., 2015; Raffin et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to Makin et al., 2013b; Makin et al., 2015; Raffin et al., 2016

claim: Increased representation of the intact hand in the missing hand cortex is a potential neural correlate of adaptive plasticity.
